How to Follow Queen’s on the BBC: A Guide to Live Coverage, Analytics, and Local Impact The 2026 Queen’s Club Championships, featuring Emma Raducanu and Serena Williams, are available on BBC Sport. Viewers can access live coverage, highlights, and analysis through the BBC Sport website and app. The event, part of the ATP and WTA calendars, runs June 12-19, with key matches streamed live. According to the official BBC Sport schedule, daily broadcasts begin at 10:00 AM BST, with prime-time slots for top-ranked players. The tournament’s inclusion of high-profile athletes like Williams, 42, and Raducanu, 23, underscores its significance as a pre-Wimbledon preparatory event. Local economic analysts note the event’s £18.7 million annual impact on London’s hospitality sector, per the 2025 Queen’s Club Economic Report.
The Strategic and Physical Demands of Queen’s: A Tactical Breakdown The Queen’s Club Championships, played on grass courts, demand a unique blend of serve-and-volley precision and baseline endurance. According to Opta Sports data, players like Raducanu, who recorded a 68% first-serve win rate at the 2024 Wimbledon warm-up, face heightened physical strain due to the surface’s low bounce. Dr. Marcus Hale, a sports biomechanist at the University of London, explains, “Grass courts increase lateral movement by 22% compared to clay, elevating ACL tear risks by 15% in high-intensity matches.” This year, Williams, whose 2025 season was derailed by a knee ligament tear, has undergone a tailored load-management program to mitigate such risks, per her agent’s statement to The Guardian .
Key matches, such as Raducanu’s opening-round clash against 14th seed Leylah Fernandez, will be analyzed using real-time xG (expected goals) metrics from the BBC’s in-house analytics team. These metrics, derived from serve speed, return accuracy, and net approaches, provide a granular view of player performance. For instance, Raducanu’s 2025 grass-court win rate of 73% against top-20 opponents highlights her adaptability to the surface, a factor that could influence her Wimbledon preparations.
“The grass court’s unpredictability forces players to balance aggression with precision. A single mis-hit volley can shift momentum in a 10-minute tiebreak,” says former ATP coach Julian Garrod, who worked with Andy Murray during his 2016 Queen’s victory.
Local Economic Ripple Effects: Hospitality, Infrastructure, and Broadcast Revenue The Queen’s Club Championships generate £18.7 million annually for London’s economy, according to the 2025 Queen’s Club Economic Report. This includes £6.2 million in hotel bookings, £3.8 million in local retail sales, and £2.1 million in temporary construction jobs for stadium upgrades. The event’s broadcast rights, sold to BBC for £9.4 million in 2024, also bolster regional media revenues. Local businesses, such as the Hilton London Bankside and The Ritz-Carlton, report a 40% surge in reservations during the tournament, per data from the London Tourism Board.

How to Access Coverage: BBC’s Digital and Broadcast Strategy Viewers can follow the tournament via BBC Sport’s live streams, which include 100% coverage of matches from the main showcourt. The BBC’s partnership with the All England Club ensures exclusive post-match interviews, tactical breakdowns, and player fitness updates. For data-driven analysis, the BBC’s in-house team provides real-time statistics, including serve speed, return placement, and shot accuracy, via the BBC Sport app.
Radio listeners can tune into BBC Radio 5 Live for live commentary, while print and digital outlets like BBC Sport offer in-depth match previews and player profiles. The event’s coverage aligns with BBC’s broader strategy to expand its sports digital footprint, which saw a 28% rise in online viewership during the 2025 Wimbledon coverage, according to internal metrics.
